docs.title: InferScale: One ML Inference Service on Three Clouds with cmx vm
docs.text: Course: COMP 488 – Cloud Computing, DevOps, and AI Team Members - Khaja Shabbir Ahmed – Cloud / DevOps Engineer (solo project) Contact kahmed5@luc.edu Instructor Gregor von Laszewski Repository https://github.com/cloudmesh-ai-luc/shabbir04 Presentation InferScale-Presentation.pdf (12 slides) Date Sep. 22, 2026

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
Problem. The same AI service often has to run on more than one cloud, but every cloud has its own way to create VMs, give them a public IP and clean them up. That makes deployments hard to repeat and clouds hard to compare fairly.

What InferScale does. InferScale is a small three-tier machine-learning service: a web frontend (nginx and a small HTML/JavaScript page), a backend that serves a sentiment-analysis model (DistilBERT) through a FastAPI REST API, and a PostgreSQL database that keeps each user's history of analyses. Each tier is its own Docker container, and the same three containers run on three clouds: Multipass on my laptop (local), Chameleon KVM@TACC (OpenStack) and AWS EC2 (public cloud). All VMs are created, reached and deleted with one tool, cmx vm from the class project cloudmesh-ai-vm, which I also contribute to. One deploy script runs the same steps on every cloud, and a load test measures how each cloud performs. On top of plain predictions, InferScale has three features: an AI review filter, live monitoring with alerts of all three clouds (Prometheus and Grafana), and multi-cloud failover. The web page and the API are protected with accounts and passwords over HTTPS.

Result. A repeatable, automated workflow and a side-by-side comparison of deployment time, response time and cost on the three clouds. Where cmx vm falls short for this workflow, I fix it in small pull requests (for example the cmx vm ip command).

docs.title: 2. Cloud Computing, DevOps, and AI
docs.text: Area How InferScale addresses it Cloud Computing Runs the same service as VMs (IaaS) on three different kinds of cloud: a local hypervisor, an OpenStack research cloud and a public cloud. Each VM runs a three-tier application: a public web frontend, a private model backend and a private database. Uses each cloud's networking (local IP, floating IP, public IP), security groups, Chameleon leases, and compares cost. cmx vm hides the differences behind one command line. Feature: multi-cloud failover. When one cloud is down, requests go to the next cloud. DevOps GitHub flow (branches, pull requests, issues), automated tests and Docker builds with GitHub Actions, a container registry, one deploy script for all clouds, a smoke test after every deployment, and clean-up so nothing keeps running. Feature: live monitoring with alerts. Every VM reports its requests, errors and response time at /metrics. Prometheus collects them from all three clouds, Grafana shows them on one dashboard, and an alert fires when a cloud stops answering or has too many errors. AI The workload is an AI model: DistilBERT sentiment analysis served for inference on CPU. The project measures how fast that model answers on each cloud. Feature: review filter. The model returns only the reviews with a chosen label (for example, negative) that it is confident about.

docs.title: 3. Requirements, Objectives & Success Criteria
docs.text: The requirements say what InferScale must do (functional) and how well it must do it (non-functional). Each one is checked by a test or a measurement (sections 5.9 and 9).

docs.title: 3.1 Functional Requirements
docs.text: ID The system must… FR-1 Classify one review (POST /api/predict): return the label and score (UNCERTAIN below an optional min_score), and save the result in the database FR-2 Filter a list of reviews (POST /api/filter) by label and minimum score FR-3 Show the signed-in account its recent analyses (GET /api/history) FR-4 Offer a web page to analyze, filter and see the history, behind a login FR-5 Answer /api/health without a login; allow /api/metrics only for owner and prometheus FR-6 Deploy and remove the service on each cloud with deploy.sh and destroy.sh, exporting the database before a VM is deleted FR-7 Send a request to the next cloud when one cloud fails (client.py) FR-8 Monitor all three clouds with alerts, and load-test each cloud

docs.title: 3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text: ID Quality Requirement NFR-1 Performance Server-side p95 under 1 second for one review, with 10 users NFR-2 Reliability At least 99 % of requests succeed, also during failover NFR-3 Security HTTPS and login; the backend and the database have no public port; no secrets in Git NFR-4 Deployability Under 15 minutes per cloud, with the same script on every cloud NFR-5 Resources and cost Runs on a 1 vCPU, 2 GB VM; $0 out of pocket and under $1 per AWS session NFR-6 Data durability The history survives container restarts (Docker volume) and is exported before a VM is deleted

docs.title: 3.3 Objectives & Success Criteria
docs.text: # Objective Success criterion 1 Package the three tiers as containers /health and /predict pass the tests; the web page shows a prediction; CI builds the web and api images (the database uses the official PostgreSQL image) 2 Run the service on three clouds using cmx vm for all VM management /predict answers on Multipass, Chameleon and AWS 3 Automate the deployment ./deploy.sh <cloud> goes from no VM to a working service with one command 4 Measure and compare the clouds A results table with deploy time, latency (p50/p95), success rate and cost per cloud 5 Improve cmx vm where the project needs it Small, reviewed pull requests to cloudmesh-ai-vm 6 AI review filter /filter returns only the reviews with the chosen label and a score at or above the threshold 7 Live monitoring with alerts One Grafana dashboard shows requests, errors and response time for all three clouds, updated every 5 seconds; an alert fires when a cloud stops answering 8 Multi-cloud failover With one cloud's VM deleted during a test run, requests still succeed through the other clouds

docs.title: 4. Scope
docs.text: In scope Out of scope Three tiers: web frontend (nginx + HTML/JavaScript), backend (FastAPI + DistilBERT) and a PostgreSQL database, each in its own container Training or fine-tuning models Three clouds: Multipass, Chameleon KVM@TACC, AWS EC2 Kubernetes and autoscaling (dropped to keep the project simple) Deploy script built on cmx vm GPUs CI with GitHub Actions High availability and 24/7 monitoring (monitoring runs only during my sessions) Load test and comparison of the three clouds Other public clouds (Azure, GCP) Small fixes to cmx vm A load balancer in front of the clouds (failover is done in the client) Three features: review filter, live monitoring with alerts, multi-cloud failover Sending alerts by email or chat (alerts are shown in Prometheus and Grafana) Login with fixed accounts over HTTPS Sign-up pages and self-service accounts; frontend frameworks such as React; a Let's Encrypt certificate (it needs a domain name) A history of analyses in a PostgreSQL database on each VM Copying the database between clouds (each cloud keeps its own history); managed databases such as AWS RDS

    CMX -->|start / ip assign / run / delete| CH[Chameleon KVM@TACC VM<br/>OpenStack]

Component Technology Notes Web frontend (web container) nginx, HTML + JavaScript Serves the web page over HTTPS, checks the login and forwards /api/ to the backend; the only public port (443) Backend API (api container) Python, FastAPI, Hugging Face Transformers Endpoints GET /health, POST /predict, POST /filter, GET /history, GET /metrics; port 8000 on the internal Docker network only Database (db container) PostgreSQL 16 (official image) Stores the history of analyses; port 5432 on the internal Docker network only; data in a Docker volume Monitoring and alerts Prometheus, Grafana (Docker on my laptop) Prometheus collects /metrics from all three clouds every 5 seconds and checks the alert rules; Grafana shows one dashboard Failover client client.py Sends each request to AWS, then Chameleon, then Multipass, until one answers Containers Docker, GitHub Container Registry Images ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-web and ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-api; the database uses postgres:16-alpine VM management cmx vm (cloudmesh-ai-vm, dev2 branch) The only tool used to create, reach and delete VMs Deployment deploy.sh Runs the same cmx vm steps on each cloud Load test Locust Runs from my laptop against each cloud

Data tier. Each VM runs its own PostgreSQL database in a third container. It stores every analysis from /api/predict (time, account, text, label and score), so each user can see their history. The database has no public port: only api reaches it, on the internal Docker network. Its data lives in a Docker volume, so it survives container restarts, and destroy.sh exports it (pg_dump) to results/<cloud>/ before the VM is deleted. Each cloud keeps its own history; copying data between clouds is out of scope, so failover still works without any data sync. Metrics, the Grafana dashboard and the load-test results stay on my laptop and in this repository.

docs.title: 5.2 Three Clouds and cmx vm
docs.text:
Why these three. Multipass is free and fast for development. Chameleon KVM@TACC is the class OpenStack cloud (project CH-817419). AWS is the most widely used public cloud, and new accounts get Free plan credits.

Local OpenStack Public Cloud Multipass on my Mac Chameleon KVM@TACC AWS EC2 cmx vm provider multipass chameleon aws VM size 1 vCPU, 2 GB (set in ~/.config/cloudmesh/clouds.yaml) m1.small (1 vCPU, 2 GB) t3.small (2 vCPU, 2 GB) OS image Ubuntu 22.04 CC-Ubuntu22.04 Ubuntu 22.04 How the service is reached The VM's local IP Floating IP The instance's public IP Port 443 (HTTPS, frontend tier) Open by default Rule added with cmx vm security-group Rule in the instance's security group Special step None cmx vm start creates a lease; end the lease after cmx vm delete Delete the instance after every session Status cmx vm VM lifecycle tested start, list, ip assign, delete tested (Oct 14) Account and credentials not set up yet

The steps deploy.sh runs on every cloud (simplified; section 5.7 adds the error handling):

cmx vm cloud set chameleon                 # multipass | chameleon | aws
cmx vm start inferscale                    # Chameleon: also creates a lease (--duration 2h)
cmx vm list                                # shows the VM and its IP
cmx vm run inferscale "curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh"
cmx vm run inferscale "sudo mkdir -p /etc/inferscale/web && cd /etc/inferscale/web && \
  sudo openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 7 -subj /CN=<ip> \
       -addext subjectAltName=IP:<ip> -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt && \
  echo <htpasswd-as-base64> | base64 -d | sudo tee htpasswd >/dev/null && \
  echo <metrics-htpasswd-as-base64> | base64 -d | sudo tee metrics.htpasswd >/dev/null && \
  sudo chown -R 101 /etc/inferscale/web"    # 101 is the nginx user in the web image
cmx vm run inferscale "sudo sh -c 'umask 077; \
  echo POSTGRES_PASSWORD=\$(openssl rand -hex 16) > /etc/inferscale/db.env'"   # made on the VM, never leaves it
cmx vm run inferscale "sudo docker network create inferscale && \
  sudo docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name db --network inferscale \
       --env-file /etc/inferscale/db.env -e POSTGRES_USER=inferscale \
       -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16-alpine && \
  sudo docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name api --network inferscale \
       --env-file /etc/inferscale/db.env ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-api:latest && \
  sudo docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name web --network inferscale -p 443:8443 \
       -v /etc/inferscale/web:/etc/nginx/secrets:ro ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-web:latest"
openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 </dev/null | openssl x509 > ~/.config/inferscale/certs/chameleon.pem
curl -f --cacert ~/.config/inferscale/certs/chameleon.pem https://<ip>/api/health   # smoke test
locust -f loadtest.py --headless -u 10 -r 2 -t 60s --host https://<ip>
cmx vm delete inferscale                   # Chameleon: then delete the lease

Only the web container publishes a port (-p 443:8443). The api and db containers have no public port; web reaches api (api:8000) and api reaches db (db:5432) by name on the private Docker network inferscale. The database data lives in the Docker volume pgdata. The database password is random, created on the VM and never leaves it. The two login files hold only password hashes; the passwords themselves stay in ~/.config/inferscale/ on my laptop (section 5.6).

On Chameleon a VM can also be started without an IP (cmx vm start inferscale --ip no) and get one later with cmx vm ip assign inferscale.

Clean-up with destroy.sh <cloud>. One script undoes a deployment: it saves the container logs (docker logs) and a database export (pg_dump) to results/<cloud>/, runs cmx vm delete inferscale, ends the lease on Chameleon, and removes the cloud's IP from targets.json and from the client's config file. Prometheus then does not raise a false CloudDown alert, and failover does not try a deleted VM.

Multi-cloud failover. deploy.sh writes each cloud's IP into a small config file. client.py tries the clouds in order, so the service keeps answering when one cloud is down:

import os
import requests

CONFIG = os.path.expanduser("~/.config/inferscale")      # outside Git
CLOUDS = ["https://<aws-ip>/api", "https://<chameleon-ip>/api", "https://<multipass-ip>/api"]
AUTH = ("client", open(f"{CONFIG}/client.password").read().strip())
CERTS = f"{CONFIG}/certs.pem"                            # the clouds' self-signed certificates

def predict(text):
    for url in CLOUDS:
        try:
            r = requests.post(f"{url}/predict", json={"text": text},
                              auth=AUTH, verify=CERTS, timeout=3)
            r.raise_for_status()   # an HTTP error, e.g. a 502 from nginx, also counts as a failure
            return r.json()
        except requests.RequestException:
            continue  # this cloud is down, try the next one
    raise RuntimeError("all clouds are down")

The demo: run requests through client.py, delete the AWS VM with cmx vm delete, and the requests keep working through Chameleon.

docs.title: 5.3 DevOps Pipeline
docs.text:
Stage Tool What it does Source GitHub One branch per change, pull requests, issues Test pytest, gitleaks, pip-audit (GitHub Actions) Unit, container and security tests, a secret scan and a dependency check on every push (section 5.9) Build Docker (GitHub Actions) Builds the two images (inferscale-web, inferscale-api) and pushes them to GitHub Container Registry Deploy deploy.sh + cmx vm Creates the VM and starts the three containers on the chosen cloud Verify curl /api/health, Locust Checks the service through the frontend tier, then measures latency Monitor Prometheus + Grafana Shows live requests, errors and response time for all three clouds, and raises an alert when a cloud is down or has too many errors Clean up cmx vm delete Removes the VM (and the Chameleon lease) after each session

The Python environment is a venv with pip, not conda, which keeps the VMs and containers clean.

Small, traceable images. The api image installs the CPU-only build of PyTorch and downloads the model when the image is built. A VM then pulls an image of about 1–2 GB (PyTorch with GPU libraries would be several GB, too big for an 8 GB disk) and does not need Hugging Face at start-up. Each image is tagged with the version from VERSION (for example inferscale-api:0.1.0), the Git commit (for example inferscale-api:3f9c2ab) and latest. Every result can be traced to the code that produced it, and a bad release can be rolled back to the last good version on all three clouds. The packages are public, so the VMs pull them without a login.

Live monitoring with alerts. Prometheus and Grafana run in Docker on my laptop (docker compose up). deploy.sh writes each cloud's IP into targets.json, and Prometheus reads the file again when it changes. Prometheus collects /api/metrics through the frontend tier of every cloud every 5 seconds and checks two alert rules:

# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: inferscale
    scrape_interval: 5s
    scheme: https
    metrics_path: /api/metrics   # nginx forwards it to the backend
    basic_auth:
      username: prometheus
      password_file: /etc/prometheus/prometheus.password   # from ~/.config/inferscale, not in Git
    tls_config:
      ca_file: /etc/prometheus/certs.pem                   # the clouds' self-signed certificates
    file_sd_configs:
      - files: [targets.json]    # one entry per cloud, e.g. {"targets": ["<aws-ip>:443"], "labels": {"cloud": "aws"}}
rule_files: [alerts.yml]

# alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: inferscale
    rules:
      - alert: CloudDown          # a cloud does not answer for 1 minute
        expr: up{job="inferscale"} == 0
        for: 1m
      - alert: HighErrorRate      # more than 5 % of requests fail for 1 minute
        expr: sum by (cloud) (rate(http_requests_total{status="5xx"}[1m]))
              / sum by (cloud) (rate(http_requests_total[1m])) > 0.05
        for: 1m

The Grafana dashboard has one line per cloud for requests per second, errors and p95 response time, and a panel that lists the alerts that are firing.

docs.title: 5.4 The Three Tiers and the Web Page
docs.text:
InferScale has three tiers. Each runs in its own container on the same VM:

Frontend tier Backend tier Data tier Container web: nginx + one HTML/JavaScript page api: FastAPI + DistilBERT db: PostgreSQL 16 Image ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-web ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-api postgres:16-alpine (official) Job Shows the web page, checks the login and forwards /api/... to the backend Runs the model, answers the API and saves each analysis Stores the history of analyses Port 443 (HTTPS, login needed), the only public port 8000, internal Docker network only 5432, internal Docker network only 
flowchart LR
    U[Browser, client.py,<br/>Locust, Prometheus] -->|HTTPS :443 + login| WEB
    subgraph VM[One VM on each cloud]
        WEB[web container<br/>nginx + web page] -->|"/api/ → api:8000 (internal network)"| API[api container<br/>FastAPI + DistilBERT]
        API -->|"SQL → db:5432 (internal network)"| DB[(db container<br/>PostgreSQL)]
    end

The page has three parts: type one review and press Analyze to see its label and score, paste several reviews and press Filter to see only the confident ones with the chosen label, or open My history to see the last 20 reviews this account analyzed. The browser asks for a user name and password first. nginx serves the page over HTTPS, checks the login, limits the request rate and passes API calls to the backend:

# nginx config in the web image (nginx's unprivileged image, runs as a normal user)
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=50r/s;

server {
    listen 8443 ssl;                                       # published as port 443
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/secrets/tls.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/secrets/tls.key;
    limit_req zone=perip burst=100 nodelay;               # too many requests -> 429
    limit_req_status 429;
    auth_basic           "InferScale";
    auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/secrets/htpasswd;     # SHA-512 hashes, no plain passwords

    location /             { root /usr/share/nginx/html; }       # the web page
    location /api/ {                                              # forward to the backend tier
        proxy_pass http://api:8000/;
        proxy_set_header X-User $remote_user;                     # the signed-in account
    }
    location = /api/health { auth_basic off; proxy_pass http://api:8000/health; }
    location = /api/metrics {                                     # only owner and prometheus
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/secrets/metrics.htpasswd;
        proxy_pass http://api:8000/metrics;
    }
}

The page calls the backend only through nginx, so the browser never talks to the model container directly:

async function analyze() {
  const text = document.getElementById("text").value;
  const r = await fetch("/api/predict", {method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
                                         body: JSON.stringify({text})});
  const {label, score} = await r.json();
  document.getElementById("result").textContent = `${label} (${score.toFixed(2)})`;
}

The page and the API come from the same address, so no CORS setup is needed, and the browser sends the login with every call.

docs.title: 5.5 AI / Model Serving (Backend Tier)
docs.text:
The model is distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english. It is small enough to run on a CPU and fit in a 2 GB VM. The core of the service:

# src/inferscale/app.py
import asyncio
import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Literal

import psycopg
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator
from transformers import pipeline

MODEL = "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
# the password comes from /etc/inferscale/db.env on the VM, never from Git
DB_URL = f"postgresql://inferscale:{os.environ.get('POSTGRES_PASSWORD', '')}@db:5432/inferscale"
SCHEMA = """CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS predictions (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    account TEXT NOT NULL, text TEXT NOT NULL, label TEXT NOT NULL, score REAL NOT NULL)"""

@lru_cache
def get_classifier():
    return pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model=MODEL)   # loaded once, then reused

def get_db():
    try:
        conn = psycopg.connect(DB_URL, connect_timeout=3)
    except psycopg.OperationalError:
        raise HTTPException(503, "database not available")
    with conn:                                           # commits when the request ends
        yield conn

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    for _ in range(30):                                  # wait up to 30 s for the db container
        try:
            with psycopg.connect(DB_URL) as conn:
                conn.execute(SCHEMA)
            break
        except psycopg.OperationalError:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
    get_classifier()                                     # load the model at start-up
    yield

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app)             # adds GET /metrics

class Review(BaseModel):
    text: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000)
    min_score: float | None = Field(None, ge=0, le=1)   # optional: below it the label is UNCERTAIN

class Reviews(BaseModel):
    texts: list[str] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    label: Literal["POSITIVE", "NEGATIVE"] = "NEGATIVE"
    min_score: float = Field(0.9, ge=0, le=1)

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(item: Review, user: str = Header("unknown", alias="X-User"),
            classifier=Depends(get_classifier), db=Depends(get_db)):
    result = classifier(item.text, truncation=True)[0]  # e.g. {"label": "POSITIVE", "score": 0.99}
    if item.min_score is not None and result["score"] < item.min_score:
        result = {"label": "UNCERTAIN", "score": result["score"]}      # not confident enough
    db.execute("INSERT INTO predictions (account, text, label, score) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
               (user, item.text, result["label"], result["score"]))   # parameters, not joined text
    return result

@app.post("/filter")
def filter_reviews(item: Reviews, classifier=Depends(get_classifier)):
    # only the confident reviews with the chosen label, e.g. the confident negative ones
    results = classifier(item.texts, truncation=True)
    return [{"text": t, **r} for t, r in zip(item.texts, results)
            if r["label"] == item.label and r["score"] >= item.min_score]

@app.get("/history")
def history(limit: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100), user: str = Header("unknown", alias="X-User"),
            db=Depends(get_db)):
    rows = db.execute("SELECT created_at, text, label, score FROM predictions "
                      "WHERE account = %s ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT %s", (user, limit)).fetchall()
    return [{"time": created.isoformat(), "text": text, "label": label, "score": score}
            for created, text, label, score in rows]

The Pydantic models check every request, so bad input gets a clear 422 error instead of crashing the service. truncation=True cuts texts that are longer than the model's limit of 512 tokens. With the optional min_score, /predict answers UNCERTAIN when the model is not confident enough. The model and the database are handed to the endpoints with Depends, so the tests can swap in fakes (section 5.9).

/metrics comes from the prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator library. It counts every request with its status code and response time, in the format Prometheus reads.

docs.title: 5.6 Security
docs.text:
Accounts and passwords. The web page and the API need a login. nginx checks it with HTTP Basic authentication, and only over HTTPS, so a password is never sent in clear text. The accounts are a fixed list that I create, so no sign-up page is needed (the database stores analyses, not accounts):

Account Used by Can use owner Me Web page, API, metrics demo The professor and the class during a demo; the password is changed after every demo Web page, API client client.py and Locust Web page, API prometheus Prometheus on my laptop Metrics only
  • Passwords are 24 random characters (openssl rand -base64 24) and live only on my laptop in ~/.config/inferscale/ (file mode 600, outside Git). The VM receives only SHA-512 hashes (openssl passwd -6), so the passwords themselves are never stored on a cloud.
  • HTTPS. deploy.sh creates a self-signed certificate for the VM's IP. My laptop saves it the first time it connects and checks it on every later call, so a fake server is rejected. Browsers show a warning once, because no authority signed the certificate; a free Let's Encrypt certificate would need a domain name, which this project does not have.
  • Rate limit. nginx allows 50 requests per second from one address (bursts up to 100) and answers 429 above that. This slows down password guessing and floods; the load test stays below the limit.
  • Network. Only port 443 is open, and only during testing. The backend has no public port: it is reached only through nginx on the internal Docker network. Every VM is deleted after each session.
  • Containers run as normal users, not root: web uses nginx's unprivileged image (port 8443 inside the container) and api runs as the user app.
  • No secrets in Git. Cloud credentials and passwords stay in ~/.config/. .gitignore blocks .env, *.pem, *.key, *.password, id_* and clouds.yaml, and CI runs a secret scan (gitleaks) and a dependency check (pip-audit) on every push.
  • Database. PostgreSQL has no public port and only api can reach it. Its password is random, created on the VM (/etc/inferscale/db.env, readable only by root) and never leaves it. The API uses parameterized SQL (values are passed separately, never joined into the query), which prevents SQL injection. nginx tells the API which account is signed in (X-User), so each user sees only their own history.
  • VM login only with SSH keys, never passwords.
  • Prometheus and Grafana run only on my laptop, and the test data is public example text with no personal data.

docs.title: 5.7 Error Handling and Readiness Checks
docs.text:
Level What can go wrong How it is handled API Missing or wrong input, a text that is too long Pydantic returns a clear 422 error; truncation=True handles long texts Login A wrong password or too many requests nginx answers 401 or 429 before the request reaches the model Database The database is still starting or goes down At start-up api waits up to 30 seconds for it; later, a request that needs it gets 503, and the db container restarts by itself Containers A container crashes Both run with --restart unless-stopped; web is restarted after api so nginx finds the new address deploy.sh A cmx vm step fails (for example "No valid host" on Chameleon) set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first error Smoke test The model needs 20–60 seconds to load curl -f retries /api/health every 10 seconds for up to 5 minutes Client A cloud is down or returns an HTTP error client.py fails over to the next cloud (raise_for_status()) Operation A cloud stops answering or many requests fail The CloudDown and HighErrorRate alerts fire

Before the first full deployment I check the parts that everything else depends on:

  • [ ] cmx vm run works on each cloud (for example cmx vm run inferscale "uname -a"). So far only start, list, ip assign and delete are tested.
  • [ ] A small test image goes the whole way: GitHub Actions → GitHub Container Registry → docker pull on a VM. The workflow's built-in token can only push under the repository owner (cloudmesh-ai-luc), so the images go there or are pushed with a personal token stored as a GitHub secret.
  • [ ] The VM disks are big enough for the image (AWS gives 8 GB and Multipass 5 GB by default).
  • [ ] Prometheus in Docker on my laptop can reach the Multipass VM's local IP.
  • [ ] The VM has a unique name in the shared Chameleon project (for example inferscale-shabbir04), so a delete can never pick another student's VM.

docs.title: 5.8 API Reference
docs.text:
All calls go to https://<vm-ip>, where nginx checks the login and forwards /api/... to the backend.

Method and path Login Request Response GET / Any account – The web page GET /api/health None – {"status": "ok"} POST /api/predict Any account {"text": "…"} (1–5000 characters), optional "min_score": 0.8 {"label": "POSITIVE", "score": 0.998}, or UNCERTAIN below min_score; the result is saved POST /api/filter Any account {"texts": ["…"], "label": "NEGATIVE", "min_score": 0.9} (1–100 texts) The matching reviews with their label and score GET /api/history?limit=20 Any account – This account's last analyses: time, text, label, score GET /api/metrics owner, prometheus – Prometheus metrics

Errors: 401 no or wrong login, 422 invalid input, 429 too many requests, 502 backend not reachable, 503 database not available.

curl --cacert ~/.config/inferscale/certs/aws.pem -u client https://<aws-ip>/api/predict \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"text": "Great movie, I loved it!"}'
# {"label":"POSITIVE","score":0.9998}

docs.title: 5.9 Testing
docs.text:
Test Tool What it checks When Unit pytest + FastAPI TestClient Each endpoint's normal answer and its 422 errors; the results of /filter and /history Every push (CI) Container docker compose up in CI, then curl The login is required and works; /api/metrics only for prometheus; an analysis shows up in the history; only port 443 is open Every push (CI) Security scan gitleaks, pip-audit No secrets in the repository; no dependency with a known vulnerability Every push (CI) Smoke deploy.sh /api/health answers after a deployment Every deployment Load, failover, alert Locust, client.py, stopping a container The targets in section 9 Measurement runs

The unit tests replace the model and the database with small fakes (FastAPI's dependency_overrides), so they run in seconds without downloading the model or starting PostgreSQL.

docs.title: 8. Risk Management
docs.text: Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation Chameleon has no free capacity ("No valid host was found") Medium Delay Retry at another time; keep sessions short A Chameleon lease keeps running after cmx vm delete High Uses allocation End the lease after every session An AWS instance is left running Low Cost Delete after every session; set a billing alert The model and the database need more memory than the VM has Medium Service crashes Use 2 GB VMs; keep PostgreSQL small; add swap or use a smaller model Credentials leak Low High Keep them only in ~/.config/, never in Git The failover demo needs two or three clouds running at once Medium More cost and allocation Keep the demo under 30 minutes and delete everything right after A password leaks (for example the demo password) Low Someone else uses the service Change it in ~/.config/inferscale/ and redeploy; change the demo password after every demo The browser warns about the self-signed certificate High The demo looks broken Explain it once and accept the certificate before the demo The history is lost when a VM is deleted Medium Lost data destroy.sh exports the database (pg_dump) first

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & Success Metrics
docs.text:
Metric How it is measured Target Deploy time (cmx vm start → first good /predict) Timer in deploy.sh Under 15 minutes on each cloud Model start-up (cold start) Timer in deploy.sh: docker run → first healthy /api/health Reported per cloud Latency p50 / p95 Locust, 60 s, 10 users (end to end), and Prometheus (time on the server only) Reported per cloud Success rate Locust At least 99 % Cost per session Provider pricing and allocation used Under $1 per AWS session Same script on all three clouds Run deploy.sh with each cloud Works without changes to the steps Review filter accuracy /filter on 20 reviews I label by hand At least 18 of 20 correct Live monitoring Grafana dashboard during a load test All three clouds shown, updated every 5 seconds Alerts Delete one cloud's VM during the failover test The CloudDown alert fires within 2 minutes Failover 200 requests through client.py, AWS VM deleted halfway At least 99 % succeed Security Calls without a password, with a wrong password, and to /api/metrics with the client account All rejected with 401; /api/health still answers History Analyze 5 reviews, restart all three containers, then open the history All 5 analyses are still listed

Each load test runs three times per cloud. The results table reports the median of the three runs, the image tag (Git commit) and the VM's CPU. The server-side time shows how much of the latency is the network between my laptop and the cloud, which keeps the comparison fair.

docs.text: Deliverable Format Backend (FastAPI + model + database access), frontend (web page + nginx) and the database schema, their Dockerfiles, and the tests in tests/ Code in this repository GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/ deploy.sh and destroy.sh built on cmx vm Scripts in this repository Review filter (/filter) and /metrics Part of the inference service Prometheus and Grafana setup (docker-compose.yml, prometheus.yml, alerts.yml, dashboard) Files in this repository, plus dashboard screenshots client.py (multi-cloud failover) Script in this repository Results table and chart for the three clouds Markdown in this repository Contributions to cmx vm Pull requests to cloudmesh-ai-vm Presentation In class

docs.title: 11. Issues
docs.text:
• AWS is not set up yet. I still need the account and credentials, and I have not tested whether the aws provider in cmx vm supports everything the deploy script needs (public IP, security group rule). If not, I open the port in the AWS console and report the gap.
  • Which Chameleon code to use. cmx vm has two versions for Chameleon: the dev2 branch and the feature/chameleon-native-chi branch. I need to know which one the project should build on.
  • Chameleon clean-up gaps. cmx vm delete does not end the lease, and releasing a floating IP fails because python-chi uses a compute call that KVM@TACC no longer supports, so IPs stay reserved.
  • Is 2 GB enough for DistilBERT, PostgreSQL and Docker together? If not, I add swap or use a smaller model.
  • The VMs are not identical (t3.small has 2 vCPUs, m1.small has 1), so the results note the differences instead of treating them as a perfectly fair comparison.
  • Failover is done in the client. It is the simplest way. A load balancer in front of the clouds would be more realistic, but it needs another VM. The cloud IPs also change with every deployment, so deploy.sh has to update the client's config file and Prometheus's targets.json each time.
